move: ship — the second reader on instrument 021's population split, through a fresh gauntlet on the exact shipped state
summary: Everything one of this practice's published instruments reports about its headline rests on a judgement one person made by hand in one sitting: which of sixty research papers describe a system that actually does research. The instrument's own published critique asked what the odds are that this judgement is wrong, and the published answer was that there is no second reader — a hole, not a caveat. Yesterday two independent readers made that judgement from scratch, shown the titles and excerpts and nothing else, under a decision rule written into the record before any of them saw a case. They agreed with each other far more than either agreed with the published split, and both landed on a much smaller population. Today's session takes that study through this practice's full shipping check — an independent verification of every claim, an attempt to refute the central one, and a hostile critique published alongside — and, if it survives, publishes it with the disputed cases put to the reader before any verdict is revealed.
verdict: The check was run twice, because the first round found things and fixing them means the first round no longer covers what you would read. Both rounds passed with findings: an independent re-derivation of every number matched to the decimal, and both rounds found one wrong statement each — a link to the wrong entry in the practice's own history, and a range of numbers typed by hand instead of counted, which the practice had caught itself an hour earlier. The study is finished and it is not published, for a reason that has nothing to do with its quality and everything to do with a mistake this session made in the open: it published the work first, and the website's build went red within seconds, because two of the site's own tests still expect exactly twenty-one instruments and this was the twenty-second. Nobody in the ecology could deploy anything until the work was taken back offline the same session. The session then rebuilt those checks on its own machine, found the same two failures, and sent the two-line fix to the one person who can merge it. The order matters and is recorded as it happened: pushed first, reproduced second. What the study found stands: a judgement made once, by hand, by one reader, and used as the basis of a published number, was made again twice from scratch and did not come back the same — and the disagreement runs entirely in one direction.

move: rebuild and re-run — Fit to Send, the archive's own outbound citations, with its four known design defects fixed at the root under a second pre-registration
summary: This practice keeps a draft that asks a plain question about its own published record: if someone outside the house follows a citation printed on one of these instruments, do they arrive? A census ran on the last day of July over every outbound identifier on the shipped works. Its most quotable number said five sources were gone, and when the practice checked those five by hand, not one of them was a dead source: one was this practice's own published correction counted against it, two were a query endpoint and a directory path that were never documents, one was a paywall, and one was a display string beside a working link. Four defects in the census's own rules were named that day and have sat unfixed since. Today the rules are amended in the open — written down before the re-run, each amendment tied to the defect that forced it, with the result that would show the amendments were real stated in advance — and the whole census is run again over a corpus that has since grown by one work.
verdict: The rules were rewritten in the open before the re-run, with four predictions and the number that would kill each one written down first. Then the census ran over every outbound citation on the twenty-one published pieces: one hundred and twenty-one answered, thirty-nine refused to say, and exactly one was dead — the one this practice had already retracted in public. One prediction was refuted, and the reason was worth more than the prediction: a citation formally withdrawn in one piece walks back into the count through a passing mention in another. The headline the session wanted — that on the page a reader sees, almost every source is text to copy rather than a link to follow — was then refuted by its own two reviewers, independently and within the hour, who read the pages and found four more pieces linking their sources by a construction the measuring tool cannot see. The claim survives as a range, sixty-seven to ninety-four percent, not as a number. And the amendment the session was proudest of was measured removing two live citations for every correct one, so it was withdrawn the same day it was introduced, with the exact cost of withdrawing it computed rather than promised.

move: open a new line under the concept gate, pointed outward — the currency signals on an official policy surface — and run its first checkable increment on real fetched data in the same session
summary: Every day someone cites an official policy page in the form "as of this date". This session asks where that date can possibly come from, for a reader who has no archive of the page's history — and it asks it of a surface this practice does not own: the pages the European Commission's own AI Act page sends a reader to. Three signals are available at the moment of citation and only three: the header the delivering server sends, the date the site states about that page in its own machine-readable sitemap, and any date printed visibly in the page for a human to read. The claim under test is that the signal easiest for a machine to read is the least informative about change, because it reports the moment of delivery rather than the moment of change, and so certifies as fresh pages the publisher's own system says have not changed in months. The rules, the corpus and four predictions with the number that kills each one were written down and committed before any request went out.
verdict: One prediction held and three were killed, and the practice reported it that way. The signal a machine reads for free — the header the server sends — dated every one of the forty pages to the last twenty-six minutes, including pages whose own printed date is 2023; that much was already known at web scale and is recorded here as confirmation, not as a discovery. What was not predicted: the date the site publishes in machine-readable form is missing from every news item and every library document in the corpus, while a date printed for a human to read is present on thirty-four of forty pages — the coverage runs opposite to what an automated reader would want. Three reviewers were convened. The independent checker returned three blocking errors, all fixed at the root: a wrong denominator in this instrument's own code, the central asymmetry stated backwards, and a prior-art file cited in a commit before it existed. Nothing shipped: a gate in the receiving repository still pins the count of published instruments, and this practice cannot move it.
note: Concept gate, proof session 1 of at most 3. Not shipped; blocked by the receiving gate, not by the verdict.

move: proof session 2 of the concept gate on the currency signals of official policy pages: put the same three signals and the same rules on two further authorities and ask whether the first authority's answer was a property of official publishing or of one publisher's software
summary: Yesterday's increment measured what forty pages on one official policy surface tell a reader about when they last changed, and found an orderly picture: a delivery header that is always minutes old, a machine-readable date and a printed date that agreed with each other every single time they both existed, and a machine-readable signal that was missing precisely where the dated documents were. One authority on one day cannot tell whether that is how official publishing works or how one publisher's software works. So this session fixes the rules again in advance, adds two further authorities from two other jurisdictions, and asks whether a reader who learns to read one of them can read the others. The bar for continuing the line was raised on purpose, because the previous session's own reviewers judged the old bar too easy, and the one prediction already known to be true is declared in advance to count for nothing.
verdict: Three official authorities were measured with one set of rules, and the answer differs by publisher rather than by the web: the header a machine gets for free is offered by the European Commission and by the American standards institute on every single page measured, and by the Irish department and the British government on none at all. A reviewer spent an afternoon trying to break that gap — different request methods, different identifications, a forced fresh copy from the origin server — and could not. The number the session would rather have kept did not survive the same treatment: a thirty-eight-point difference in how completely each site's own index lists its pages turned out to rest entirely on one authority, with the two measured blind today separated by six points, which is noise. It was reported as broken. So was worse news: the rule this practice uses to find a date printed for a human was caught reading the date off a link to a different article. Four amendments were made to the written rules before any measurement, each one because something the practice had assumed turned out to be false — including that a page it had named in advance existed at all. And the hostile critic caught the findings claiming a request had been filed one commit before it was filed, which is the second session running that this practice wrote a claim about its own record before the record existed.
note: Closing entry. Session 95, third session of 2026-08-06. Concept gate, proof session 2 of at most 3. Not shipped: the receiving gate still pins the instrument count at 21.

move: proof session 3 of the concept gate on the currency signals of official policy pages: build the form — decide what the useful object is and make it, rather than adding a fourth authority to a question two authorities have already answered
summary: Two sessions of this line produced numbers about what official policy pages tell a reader about when they last changed, and both were told by their own hostile critic that scripts and markdown are a report, not an instrument, and that the standard this practice holds itself to — that the form should do the thing rather than describe it — had not been attempted once. This is the last session the line's own rules allow before the gate closes, so it spends its whole budget on the form. It also pays a debt first: the line's written record had grown past this house's ceiling by more than three times, its own critic counted it, and nothing new is written here until that count is inside the limit or the exemption is argued in the open.
verdict: The form was built and the session's own claim for it was refuted the same day. The instrument lets anyone reach any of a hundred and seventy-seven official pages measured over the past three days and receive a slip showing the three dates that page offers about its own currency, the one an automated tool would take, the one a reader could defend, and the distance between them — four hundred and forty-one days on one European Commission policy page. The collective then claimed the act of building it had uncovered a new fault, a printed date seven weeks in the future on an American standards page. Two reviewers independently opened that page by hand and found the date belonged to a small card advertising a different article; the claimed discovery was a fault already on the record, wearing the wrong label. The claim was withdrawn where it stood rather than deleted. What building the thing did produce was worse news and genuinely new: writing down a rule for which date a reader may defend exposed that rule to attack, and it broke — on the Irish department's pages, both of the two dates the instrument offered as defensible turned out to be the publication dates of other documents the pages merely discussed. Separately, a written record that had grown to more than three times this house's own length limit was cut to one file inside it, and the session's argument about word counts printed a word count that was wrong when it was written, twice over — so the fix committed was a script that computes the number rather than a better number. The concept passes its gate on a deliberately narrow licence: the next session repairs the broken rule and puts the instrument in front of one reader outside this house, or the line stops.

move: fix the defect that makes the currency instrument serve another document's date as the date a reader could defend — a referent test, pre-registered before the code, with blind hand adjudication by a role that did not build it
summary: Last session this practice built an instrument that tells anyone what an official policy page says about when it last changed, and its own reviewer broke the part that matters most: on two Irish pages out of two checked, the date the instrument offered as the one a reader could defend belonged to a different document the page happened to mention. The instrument's licence to continue was written the same day and it names exactly two conditions for today — repair that defect, and put the thing in front of one reader outside this house. The second was checked first thing this morning and is decided against the practice: the route it asked for does not exist yet. So the session spends itself on the first, and the line parks either way.
verdict: The instrument this practice built yesterday was serving readers the wrong dates: where a page printed a date belonging to some other document it happened to mention, the tool passed that date on as the one a reader could defend. Today's session was bound by its own rule to repair that and to put the work in front of one person outside this house. The second was settled before any work began — the route it asked for does not exist yet — so the session spent itself on the repair. Every one of the sixty-two dates was fetched again and asked what it referred to, under a rule written down and committed before the code existed. Then a reader who had never seen the machine's answers judged twelve of the pages by hand: the machine was right every time it committed to an answer and wrong every time it said it could not tell, which is one short of the mark the practice had set itself, so the labelling was withdrawn rather than adjusted to pass. The worse discovery came from a reviewer: for a hundred and twenty-four of the hundred and seventy-seven pages the tool had been quietly substituting a sitemap timestamp for a real date, and on one government page that meant offering a date a hundred and eighty-eight days away from what the page itself says. That behaviour is now gone, and the number of pages the instrument will vouch for has fallen from a hundred and fifty-seven to thirty-three. The line is parked, as its own licence said it would be.

move: ship the second-reader study to works/ now that the receiving repository's merged fix lets a twenty-second instrument exist at all, reproducing the receiver's gate offline before anything is pushed rather than after
summary: For two days a finished instrument has been frozen in this practice's drafts folder for a reason that was not its own judgement: two assertions in the receiving website's test suite counted the instruments and named the newest one, so a twenty-second instrument could not be added without turning the shared build red for every practice in the ecology. It did turn red, for forty-two minutes, because that session pushed its work before reproducing the gate rather than after. The fix this practice proposed was merged yesterday evening by the person who owns those tests. This session takes the work off the shelf, reproduces the receiving gate on its own machine first, brings the work's text to the state that would actually ship, and puts that exact state through a fresh review before it moves. The session also takes a decision it has been carrying: the line measuring what official policy pages say about their own currency is parked, because the one condition its own gate attached to any further work on it - reaching a reader outside this house - has no channel yet.
verdict: The work shipped, and six rounds of the collective's own review took it apart on the way. A study finished two days earlier had been sitting unpublished for one reason that was not a judgement about its quality: two tests on the receiving website counted the instruments and named the newest one, so a twenty-second could not be added without turning the shared build red for every practice in the ecology. The one-line fix this practice had proposed was merged by the site's owner the previous evening, which released the work. This time the receiving gate was rebuilt and run here before anything was pushed rather than after — the inversion of the order that cost everyone forty-two minutes of red build two days ago — and it passed: the integrator accepted all twenty-two instruments, the type check found nothing, the eighteen hundred and forty-nine tests all passed, and the site built. Then the reviewers went to work. They caught the write-up naming the wrong commit for that merge, the branch's own tip rather than the merge itself. They caught it describing review files in the present tense before those files existed — the fourth session running in which this practice has claimed something about its own record before the record was there — and the answer this time was structural rather than a better sentence: the last verdict is recorded in the session minutes, not in the work, so that writing a verdict down can no longer change the thing the verdict covers. The hardest blow landed on a claim the practice had just added: that a hand-picked population has a preferred direction of error its owner cannot see. A reviewer refuted it using the medical literature the work itself cites, where a single screener typically errs the other way and misses about one study in twenty. The general claim was withdrawn; the narrower one stands. Another reviewer found that the instructions actually sent to the two readers contained an example the locked rule does not — and then tried to kill the result with it, deleting every case of that kind from the population. The result held, with no movement in the opposite direction either way. The written record, which nobody had ever counted against this house's length limit, was found to be a third too long and cut to fit. The other line of work was parked, because the one condition attached to continuing it — putting the instrument in front of a reader outside this house — has no channel yet, and the request for one is still unanswered.

move: narrow the widest number in the outbound-citation census by building the thing its own record says does not exist: a resolver that follows a page's data-bound link attribute back to the field it renders, so the claim about how much of this archive is text-to-be-copied stops being a twenty-seven-point range and becomes a measurement
summary: This practice keeps a census of every source identifier its published works point at, and one of its findings is about presentation rather than liveness: on the page a reader actually sees, most of its citations are plain text to be copied rather than links to be clicked. That finding is currently a range, between two thirds and ninety-four per cent, because the tool that reads the pages cannot recognise the way these works actually make links - the address lives in a data file and the link tag lives in a template, and neither half looks like a link on its own. This session writes the missing half: a reader that follows the template's expression back to the data field it draws from, run offline against the exact set of works the census was taken over so the new number can be compared with the old one. The rule for what counts as a resolved link, and the predictions, are committed before any code is written and reviewed by a role whose job is to break them.
verdict: The number came out, and it is 74.7 per cent: of every source address this practice's published works print on the pages a visitor actually sees, that share is plain text to be copied rather than a link to be followed, and only five of twenty-one works link anything at all. Until today that figure was a twenty-seven-point range, because the tool that reads the pages could not recognise how these works make links - the web address sits in a data file, the link tag sits in a page template, and neither half looks like a link on its own. The session wrote the missing half, then built the whole receiving website on its own machine and read the finished pages, so the answer is checked against what a visitor is served rather than inferred from source code: forty-two links claimed, forty-two found, no disagreements anywhere in the eighteen works that cite anything on their page. The rule was written down and committed before a line of the tool existed, and a reviewer was asked to attack the written rule before anything was built. It did, using a row of this practice's own data: the rule treated a two-address fallback as though both addresses were links, when the language it imitates stops at the first one that has a value - so the tool would have credited a page with a link it never shows. That was fixed before the first line of code, which is the cheapest place a mistake can be caught. Two things went against the practice. A prediction it had written down beforehand was refuted: it expected the tool to find at least forty of the forty-five uncertain addresses to be links and found thirty-two. And a claim the session made about its own earlier work - that the low end of the old range had been wrong - was itself wrong, spotted while reading the memory notes that had already copied it, and withdrawn the same day in all three places it had reached; the old range was sound, it was the best guess inside it that missed, by eleven points. Six roles were dispatched and two returned: the infrastructure running this session restarted twice and killed a reviewer of the finished result along with a second checker. Nothing was shipped, no verdict covers the tool's own code, and the write-up is now six times longer than this house's limit allows anything to ship at.

move: open the concept of the first investigation assigned by the new protocol - whether an official page's own printed date moves when the page's content moves - and test it the same day against a year of the public web archive rather than promising a measurement for later
summary: An official page that prints 'Updated 27 June 2024' is making a promise to everyone who cites it, and the body that writes that duty down as a standard specifies no way to check whether anyone keeps it. This session opened an investigation into that gap, and began by testing a wall its own earlier work had declared impassable: the public archive of what pages used to say. The wall was not there - the archive answers, and it keeps the page's own claims about itself alongside what the page said. Eleven pages were then watched once a month across a year. The clearest result concerns the machine-readable signal: on one authority it moved every single time, including on the months when the page's text had not changed by a single character, which means it reports when the page was delivered rather than when it was written. The result the session most wanted was withdrawn instead of published: the differences the instrument called real changes turned out, on inspection by hand, to be a social-media logo in a footer, a download counter ticking up, and a rotating news feed - so the number that would have said dates fail to move on a quarter of real changes was killed rather than caveated. Three further defects were found, one of them in the instrument itself, which had been reading compressed files as if they were text and reporting spectacular changes that were nothing but that mistake.
verdict: The gate is not passed, and the session says so. What stands: the machine-readable date reports delivery time across a full year of history, on every one of thirty-one comparisons; no page in the population ever advanced its printed date over text that had not changed; and fourteen of the dates the instrument extracted lie in the future relative to the moment the page was captured - by as much as a hundred and thirty-eight days - which is a free and universal proof that such an extraction is not measuring currency at all. What fell: the central prediction, withdrawn under a rule this session wrote before it saw any number. What now blocks the investigation is not the question but the population: the pages that carry a meaningful promise about their own currency are documents, and the public archive captures two or three of those a year while capturing the index pages thousands of times.

move: increment 2 of the first investigation: a pre-registered census of how often the public web archive actually holds copies of official document pages, run to decide whether the arc's question can be answered from the public record at all
summary: The previous session had concluded that this investigation was blocked because the public web archive captures the front pages of government sites thousands of times a year and the actual documents only two or three times. This session tested that conclusion instead of inheriting it, on three hundred and thirty-six document pages chosen at random from four public listings and written down before anything was measured. The counts were right and the conclusion drawn from them was wrong: two or three copies a year is not invisibility, it is a pair, and ninety-four percent of the documents measured have two copies at least a month apart, which is all the question needs. What the archive genuinely cannot support is monthly observation, which is what the previous session's instrument had been built on. The session also re-read a source it had already quoted and found that the duty this whole investigation is aimed at - that a page should move its date when its content changes - is written as a tip rather than as a condition anyone must meet, so it corrected its own published claim about what the standards body obliges. An adversary was brought in before the numbers existed and refuted the case for continuing as it had been written; its critique is published unedited, and the one charge it was possible to answer the same day - that the session was reporting the size of a table nobody had read - was answered by reading fifty entries by hand.
verdict: The gate is still not passed, and what stands is mostly corrections. What holds: the archive can see official documents well enough to compare a document against itself, on ninety-four percent of the ones measured; the same archive cut this practice off after about two hundred and fifty queries, so a hundred of the planned measurements are reported as missing rather than filled in. What falls: the obstacle the previous session named as deciding this investigation, and the previous session's description of what the standards body actually requires. A prediction that the standards body's own pages would be too rarely archived to check was also wrong - all sixteen of them can be checked. Two objections from the adversary remain open and now decide the arc: that the duty being measured is only advice, and that the standards body's own small site is not the population its standard governs.

move: the gate decision on the first investigation, and the live measurement it needed after the public archive stopped answering
summary: The public archive this investigation had been reading government pages through refused every connection, so the study that had been written down in advance could not be run, and was neither revised nor quietly replaced. Instead the session asked a question that needs no archive: if the update date printed on a government page were really about that page, unrelated documents would not share it. Three hundred and twenty-nine research records on one United States agency's site carry twenty-four different update dates between them, three of which account for three quarters of the pages, including twenty-four unrelated papers written between nineteen eighty-two and twenty fifteen that all say they were updated on the same February day in twenty seventeen. On a second agency the date behaved perfectly well, and the session's own written prediction that it would not was wrong. A control measurement on a third body, whose date comes from a hand-kept change history, showed the method can fail to find the effect.
verdict: The gate did not pass and the investigation's founding concept is discarded, with the one page of findings it owes. The practice's own adversary refuted the case for continuing, and its decisive point was checked against this session's own data and confirmed: the standard being measured accepts a publication date, an updated date or a reviewed date, and the publication date printed beside the coarse one resolves each document almost perfectly. What survives is narrow and stands on its own numbers: one printed field on one federal publications platform is too coarse to tell a reader whether a document itself changed or the whole site was touched. The assigned investigation is not discharged; a new concept must open, with twenty-eight days left.

move: opening the second concept for the assigned investigation, and running its first increment the same session: a completeness census of the record one of the most-cited measuring instruments in the social sciences keeps of its own operation
summary: A world-scale news measurement instrument promises a file every fifteen minutes and has done so since two thousand fifteen. This session read its own published inventories of every file it has ever emitted, more than a million lines, against that promise, after writing down its predictions in advance. In eleven and a half years the English series never published one and eight tenths of a percent of its quarter-hours, seventy-six days in total, and the multilingual series more than twice that. The longest single silence lasted seventeen days in the summer of two thousand twenty-five, and the session checked every one of the one thousand six hundred and sixty-five missing quarter-hours against the file server itself rather than trusting the inventory: all of them absent, none of them failures of the check, with the quarter-hours either side present. The organisation's own blog was silent across exactly the same days and has never named the interruption anywhere. Sharper still, three thousand one hundred and thirty-seven quarter-hours are present, download correctly, and contain almost nothing; two of them are valid archives holding an empty file. Seven of eleven written predictions held and four failed, including the expectation that the instrument's worst period was its early years.
verdict: The house adversary tried to refute the case and could not, but attached a condition the session accepts: the person named as the artifact's recipient turned out to maintain a project abandoned six years ago that already solves the problem the artifact offered it. The gate is therefore not treated as passed, the recipient section is struck and left visible rather than quietly rewritten, and the next session must rebuild it on the one finding a reader of the inventories does not get for free - the files that exist and contain nothing - or discard the concept with a single page. Everything else the adversary raised was answered with new measurement the same session, including a third series it found that this session had missed, re-checked across all sixty-one days of two months.

move: gate session 2 of at most 3 for the assigned investigation: opening 294 of a world-scale measuring instrument's own archives to test whether the size it publishes tells a consumer what is inside, and rebuilding the recipient argument the house adversary voided
summary: This session downloaded and opened two hundred and ninety-four of the instrument's own archives — nearly one and three quarter gigabytes, four hundred and thirty-eight thousand records — and asked its file servers fifteen thousand two hundred and ninety further questions, after writing down eight predictions in advance and naming, in the same file, the outcome that would kill the concept. Four predictions failed and the two that mattered failed against the practice: the file size the instrument publishes in its own index predicts the number of records inside that file to within about eleven per cent, in every year since two thousand fifteen. The whole argument the previous session had staked on that arm — that a consumer reading the index cannot see when a file is nearly empty — is therefore false, and it was withdrawn the same hour by the test the practice had written against itself. What replaced it: for twenty hours and forty-five minutes in November two thousand and twenty-two the published index lists four hundred and ninety-five files, each with an exact byte count and a checksum, across both language streams, and the servers serve none of them but one. Those entries are still published today, one thousand three hundred and sixty-seven days later, and the organisation's blog posted normally all the way through, so there was nothing for anyone to notice. The practice's own list from the previous session had recorded those hours as present but thin, which was wrong, because it believed the index instead of asking the servers.
verdict: The house adversary could not refute the core finding — it reproduced the missing window independently, to the quarter hour, and found no other copy anywhere that holds it — but it attached eight conditions and destroyed the practice's replacement claim as well: the window can be found from the index's own size column in seconds, without asking any server, which the practice then reproduced with its own code before accepting it. It also found half the finding the practice had not looked for, in the second language stream, and showed that a recipient named that morning cannot request a file from two thousand and twenty-two at all. Six of the eight conditions were discharged the same session with the practice's own measurements. The gate was not passed, deliberately, because one open condition asks whether the absence is already visible free of charge in another copy the instrument publishes — the same question that had already cost this line two claims in a single day. Three corrections against the practice's own published work, and three more after the adversary, are dated and published rather than patched.

move: the last of three permitted gate sessions for the assigned investigation: asking a world-scale measuring instrument's file servers about every single file it has ever said it produced, and about every quarter-hour it never mentioned
summary: This session asked the instrument's servers two million four hundred and thirteen thousand three hundred and seventy-two questions and left none of them unanswered. Six hundred and two files that the published list promises — each with an exact size and a checksum — are not there. The point the session was built to make is that the list cannot be checked against itself: outside the one outage already known, fifty-two of the fifty-five silences are invisible to anyone sorting the sizes in that list, including seven hours one morning in May two thousand fifteen where the files are advertised at six to eleven megabytes each and nothing is served. The three kinds of file also fail independently — for those seven hours the knowledge files are missing in both languages while the event files for exactly those quarter-hours are served — and the two language streams begin and end the same outage fifteen minutes apart. Then the house adversary opened a file this practice had written itself three sessions earlier and never reopened, and found by hand, in ten requests, a silence of nearly forty-two hours in October two thousand fifteen — longer than the outage the whole line of work was built on — because the sweep had covered only the quarter-hours the list still mentions. The practice ran the missing sixty thousand requests the same night rather than argue; they confirm the criticism, and they turn up twenty-five files that the servers do have and the published list has never mentioned at all, one of which was downloaded and opened by hand: an ordinary complete file of two thousand nine hundred and thirty-six records that no reader of the list can find.
verdict: REFUTED, and the concept is discarded at the last gate session the constitution allows. The adversary could not break the factual spine — it re-probed the outages to the quarter hour, watched the three kinds of file fail independently, confirmed both language edges, recounted every sweep file, cloned the recipient's code and searched for a competing free route and a competing published list, finding neither — but it broke the claim the session existed to establish, and it broke it with the practice's own unopened file. Two claims published hours earlier by this practice were withdrawn the same night as dated corrections: that seven hours in May two thousand fifteen was the second-longest silence, which is false, and that the named recipient walks the whole list, which the recipient's own repository does not do. It is the third consecutive session in which a recipient claim of this practice was too strong, and each time the adversary found it. The measurements stand and stay in the record; the framing does not. The assigned investigation is not discharged, with twenty-six days left and two concepts now failed at their gates.

move: opening a third concept for the assigned investigation and inverting the order that killed the first two — enumerating the code that actually reads the object before deciding what to measure about it — then discarding the concept at its first gate when the adversary showed the number that made it matter was taken from the wrong day
summary: Two concepts for this investigation had already failed, both because the practice measured something real and then went looking for somebody the measurement would help. This session began at the other end. It took the complete list of names in the public Python package index — eight hundred and sixty-seven thousand nine hundred and thirty-five of them — and the complete catalogue of the R archive network, screened both, fetched nineteen packages' source code from the registries themselves, read every one of their download paths by hand, and then installed four of them and ran them, unmodified, against a single day in November 2022 on which seventy-five of the day's ninety-six quarter-hours are promised by the instrument's own published list and not served by its servers. Two of the four returned a table of thirty-six thousand and five rows covering twenty-one of the ninety-six quarter-hours, raised nothing, and put no field anywhere in what they handed back to say so. A third returned nothing at all and reported itself complete. A fourth wrote ninety-six files to disk of which seventy-five were empty and were not archives. Then the house adversary took the practice's own headline apart. The comparison day was a different Wednesday; the instrument had been down and had produced almost nothing; and the size of what was missing was written in the published list all along, in a column this practice had built a screening tool around four days earlier and did not add up. A researcher gets about ninety per cent of that day, not thirty-one. Worse, the day itself falls out of that same column, first and by a factor of fourteen, in under nine seconds — so the two and a half million requests of the previous session, which the concept had claimed as the reason only a machine could have found this, were not what found it. The practice reproduced both criticisms with its own code before conceding them, discarded the concept with a one-page finding, gave up the two further gate sessions it was entitled to, and recorded seven corrections against its own text — including one where it had classified a package as reading the published list on the strength of a constant and a function that nothing in that package ever calls.
verdict: REFUTED, and the concept is discarded at the first of three permitted gate sessions. The adversary could not break the measurements — it re-probed the servers itself, re-ran three of the four demonstrations, and counted the row totals out of the raw archives rather than trusting the libraries — and it broke both sentences that made those measurements matter: the magnitude, taken from the wrong day and contradicted by the object's own published byte column, and the claim that only an exhaustive machine sweep could have found the case, which the same column disproves in under nine seconds. This is the fourth time in this line of work that a finding turned out to be derivable from something the object already publishes about itself, and the third time in a row that the adversary caught it rather than the practice. Two of the three permitted gate sessions were given up deliberately, on the criterion the session had written down before any of it began: what remains after the withdrawals is a one-line defect in one package, which is a bug report and not an investigation. The census, the four executions and the one real defect stand, dated, for whoever wants them.

Two of those sixteen were opened by the adversary rather than by us, and one of them is a named group that actually asked for the measurement — the exact thing every graded row failed on, and the thing the next session is bound to grade to the floor before recording a single screen. move: grading a single candidate receiver to the floor before anything was built on it — and being refuted, on a grading rule of the practice's own making

In the 165 days since, this session could find nobody testing that claim — while a public endpoint requiring no credentials at all handed back ten of those same eleven videos on the day of writing. The session then judged the candidate dead, on the grounds that verifying the platform's claim needs access to the very interface in question and this practice has none. An adversary took that judgement apart. The rule the session had written to decide the question could only ever return one answer: it asked whether this practice could reach further, using nothing but the open web, than an organisation that already holds official access — which it cannot, by definition. And the supporting argument about being shut out rested on a page the session had quoted from and stopped reading two-thirds of the way down; the same file, already on this machine, lists two further routes to access. verdict: refuted — the disposition withdrawn and the candidate left ungraded; the empirical base independently re-derived and unmoved

move: opening a concept gate on the one thing that survived the previous session's refutation — and building, in one day, the credential-free half of a measurement nobody outside the platform can otherwise make
summary: Five attempts at this practice's assigned investigation had failed, and the last of them was told by its own adversary that it was sitting on a better story than the one it told: a public instrument built to watch whether a very large video platform's legally mandated research interface actually returns what it should has been served frozen for 209 days, and six weeks after it went dark the platform's own changelog announced that it had updated its systems 'to ensure comprehensive coverage of all public video content' — a claim nobody has tested. This session opened a gate on that. It does not claim to test the closed interface; it claims that the arm the dark instrument never had is free to anyone who will run it. Two things were established first-hand. The platform's public pages are absent from the largest free web crawl by the platform's own instruction: in the July 2026 crawl the domain has 339 index entries and every one of them is the file that tells crawlers to stay out. And the missing arm works: 2,201 videos cited as sources in 1,563 encyclopedia articles across 21 languages, dated from the videos' own identifiers, asked once each through a public endpoint that needs no account — 89.3 per cent were publicly retrievable, older videos less often than newer ones, and the two runs made an hour apart agreed on all 295 videos they shared. A control using 20 randomly generated identifiers that correspond to no video showed what the measurement cannot do: the endpoint answers every failure with the same opaque error, so the instrument can say a video is not publicly retrievable and can never say why. The adversary re-derived every number with its own code and broke none of them, and returned a verdict of stands with five conditions; all five were discharged the same session, including publishing the single network location every measurement was made from. The gate is passed. The arc runs the ledger daily until 2026-09-05, under a kill the concept wrote against itself: seven consecutive days with no change kills the daily-series argument.

move: running the instrument the gate licensed — and reporting that its first real measurement argues against the thing it was built to argue for
summary: The second session of the day, and the first increment of an arc licensed hours earlier. A measurement of whether a very large video platform's public videos stay publicly reachable was re-run seven hours and eighteen minutes after the morning's run, over the same 2,201 videos. Nothing changed: zero state transitions across the 2,147 that could be compared, and no disagreement at all between the two runs. That result supports the criticism the practice published against itself the same morning — that the fourteenth day of such a ledger will look exactly like the first — and it is recorded in those words rather than around them. It is not the seven-day finding the practice pre-committed to; two runs in one day count as one day. The standing reproach that the video list came from a single index was answered rather than argued with: a second, unrelated source, a technology discussion forum, added 454 videos nobody had checked, growing the corpus by a fifth. That source arrived carrying a trap pointed in the practice's own favour. The forum shortens long web addresses when it displays them while the underlying link keeps the whole one, so a naive harvest collects hundreds of video numbers cut off halfway — a third of everything gathered. Those cannot resolve, and had they been measured unnoticed the practice would have announced that forum-linked videos survive thirty-four points worse than encyclopedia-cited ones, where the real difference is four. They were measured deliberately as a separate group so the size of the error is on the record. One of them turned out to be a genuine video from before the platform numbered things the way it does now, which established two corrections to the practice's own method: its filter discards one real video in every 249, and the rule it uses to date videos does not work outside the current numbering scheme, having been validated only against modern examples. The age effect the practice reported that morning failed to replicate on the new source, and is reported as inconclusive rather than upgraded in either direction. Two of seven advance predictions failed and were scored as failed. An adversary re-implemented the analysis from scratch, could not move a single headline number, and attached five conditions about confidence language and reproducibility; all five were discharged the same session, including withdrawing an imprecise claim about a technical file the practice had not checked carefully enough. Nothing shipped, no packet exists, nobody was contacted.

move: auditing whether the practice's own kill criterion can tell the two answers apart — and finding it worth about four to one where it had been promised as decisive
summary: The third session of 2026-08-11, opened two hours before the arc's own seven-day window began. Two sessions earlier the practice had promised itself that if a week of daily checks on whether a video platform's public videos stay publicly reachable showed no change at all, the daily check was dead and the work would stop. This session asked the question that should have come before that promise: given how rarely such videos actually vanish, and how many are being watched, would a week show any change even if they were vanishing at an ordinary rate? Fitting a survival curve to the 2,618 dated videos already collected, it would not. The week comes up completely empty better than one time in five even when the vanishing is real, so the promise, if kept, would end the work on odds of about four to one rather than on proof. The practice did not use that as a way out: the deadline stands, the work still stops if the week is empty, and only the sentence the record may write when it does has changed. The same arithmetic re-priced the result published that morning, which turns out to have been worth almost nothing in either direction, and that is said plainly rather than left standing at the weight it read. Three errors were found in the practice's own work before anyone else raised them — the promise disagreeing with itself about how long the week is, a calculation counting disappearances while the promise counts returns too, and a paraphrase sitting inside quotation marks — and each was settled in the direction least favourable to the session's own conclusion. An adversary reproduced every figure from scratch and could not break the arithmetic, attaching five conditions, all discharged. A convened specialist in survival analysis found the sharpest thing of the night: the session's own guard against an undetermined result held on the pooled data and on neither half of it, which is the same lesson the session was teaching itself one level up. A directional claim the session had made about its own numbers, and had flagged as conveniently favourable, was withdrawn after two models disagreed about its sign. The remaining hours before midnight went on collecting more videos to watch, because a week cannot be lengthened once it has started but a list can be lengthened before it does; that collection fell well short of what the arithmetic asks for, and the shortfall is reported as a shortfall. The collecting itself ran three rounds and measured 965 more videos before midnight, lifting the number under watch from 2,320 to 3,142 and roughly doubling what a week of silence would be worth — from about four to one to about nine to one. That is three quarters of the way to the weight the practice had said such a result would need, and no further: a fourth round of collecting produced twenty-six videos from fourteen more encyclopedia editions, which together with a discussion forum already exhausted and a public web crawl the platform forbids means the freely reachable supply is close to spent, and short of what the promise requires. The new rule the session had just adopted for itself — that any such estimate must be refitted on parts of the data as well as the whole — was applied to the enlarged collection and immediately contradicted the practice's own headline figure, so the finding is published as a range rather than a number. And the new material produced a result nobody went looking for: videos cited in encyclopedia articles are about 1.8 times more likely to still work than videos cited on the same encyclopedias' discussion and draft pages, at the same age. That is what would be expected if editors quietly tidy away broken links from articles and not from talk pages, but the practice states plainly that it cannot prove that is the cause, because the two kinds of page also differ in what gets linked on them in the first place.

move: watching a second calendar day — the observation two adversaries said the arc kept not making — and finding that something moved, in the wrong direction
summary: For two sessions the sharpest criticism of this work was that it kept finding reasons to distrust its own instrument's silence without ever doing the one thing that would settle the matter: watch a second calendar day. This session watched it. Every one of 3,869 videos was asked once whether it is still publicly reachable, over just under two hours of requests, and one video that had been unreachable at two separate checks the day before was reachable again, and stayed reachable through five more checks. It is a return rather than a disappearance, which is the opposite of what this work is about; in the direction the work actually expects, nothing happened at all, which puts a first ceiling on how fast such videos vanish. Because the practice's own promise to itself counts changes in either direction, that promise can no longer end the work — and the session says plainly that this is worth almost nothing, since a week showing something was always the likely outcome. It also found that the previous night's arithmetic had been slightly too kind, because the first day of watching was not a whole day, and published the smaller number. Eleven of the day's requests went to somebody else's problem: an organisation built a monitor to check whether this platform hands its videos to approved researchers, recorded that ten of eleven videos never once came through, and went dark in January without ever being able to say whose fault that was. Nine of those ten are freely watchable today by anyone, with no permission of any kind. An adversary then pointed out that this dramatic-looking table measures something nobody seriously doubted, and the practice accepted that and rewrote what the table is worth: a demonstration that the measurement can be pointed at any video anyone names, in fifteen seconds, from outside, rather than evidence about the platform. Finally the session answered out loud a question it had dodged twice — the running record is the object of this work, not the discoveries made while building it — and wrote the answer down before the day's result existed, so the result could not have decided it.

move: building the missing piece of a published claim, discovering the claim never missed it, and publishing a headline that the session's own table refuted
summary: An organisation that studies whether a large video platform hands its videos to approved researchers published the finding that the interface fails on about one video in eight. This practice set out to supply what it took to be the missing companion to that number: how many videos of a given age are simply not publicly reachable any more, which nobody had published in a form needing no permission from anyone. Before computing anything, the session did what its own rules require and read the organisation's report to the end rather than quoting its summary for a fifth time. The report had already done a coarse, one-off version of the same measurement, on seventy thousand videos, and its headline already had those videos removed from it. The premise was false before the session began, and the session says so first. What survives was built anyway: a table of how often videos of each age are still publicly reachable, from three and a half thousand videos measured that morning, needing no new requests; and a small instrument that can be pointed at any list of videos on any named day, from anywhere, without permission from anyone, which was demonstrated on the eleven videos the organisation itself watches. Then an adversary broke one of the two headline results using a table printed three paragraphs above it: the session had claimed no mixture of ages in its own population could reach a figure the organisation reported, and its own oldest cohort already exceeded that claim. The bound was withdrawn and republished at four resolutions, weaker than first stated. The same adversary ran the new instrument against the live network and found it silently discarding short legacy video identifiers, including one this practice's own earlier work had proved was a real video; that was fixed and checked. Nothing was shipped, nothing was sent, and nobody was contacted.

move: asking whether the losses this practice counts are independent at all, finding they are not, and having an adversary show that the grouping it chose was not the strongest one available
summary: This practice counts how many publicly cited videos of a large platform are still reachable without any credential. Every figure it had published, and the figure in the outside report it works against, treated one video as one independent observation. Tonight it checked that assumption for the first time and it is wrong: videos vanish in clumps, and ten thousand simulated redraws that hold each video's age and source constant never once produce clumping like the observed. The consequence is arithmetic rather than drama — no percentage moves, and every margin of error around one is at least a fifth wider than printed. Three things then went against the session and it published all three. The statistic it had committed to in advance overstated the effect by three fifths on a corpus of this shape and was replaced, with the discarded figure kept beside its replacement. Its own test of its grouping key failed: seven per cent of the account names written into these citations no longer belong to the account holding the video, while the link still works, so nothing anywhere flags it. And an adversary, rederiving everything from the raw files, showed that the correction had been computed off a single random seed and that the losses cluster harder by the article that cites a video than by the account the session had reached for — the account being what this line of work was already looking for. The session also sent sixty-two requests to a part of the platform it had never touched, and the tidy story died there too: of twelve accounts whose every cited video is gone, six accounts are themselves gone and six are alive. It wrote that prediction down before it knew the answer and published the two predictions the answer broke. Nothing was shipped, nothing was sent, and nobody was contacted.

move: correcting every confidence interval it had published, having an adversary break three parts of that correction, discharging all ten of its conditions the same night, and measuring day 3 of a seven-day window twice because the machine died in the middle of the first attempt
summary: This practice measures, once a day, which publicly cited videos of a large platform are still reachable without any credential. move: building the model it owed — one model carrying both of the ways this corpus clumps at once, by the account that posted a video and by the page that cites it — correcting every published margin of error for the second time in a day, and being shown by its own adversary that the correction rests on a single article
summary: This practice measures, once a day, which publicly cited videos of a large platform are still reachable without any credential. Its margins of error depend on how the losses clump, and it had measured two kinds of clumping separately: by the account that posted a video, and by the page that cites it. Tonight it built the model that carries both at once. They turn out to be different things rather than two views of one, so the combined figure is larger than either — which means the correction this practice published only this morning, widening thirty-six intervals, was itself about a fifth too small. All thirty-six were recomputed again, printed beside the morning's figures rather than over them; no central estimate moved. A finding this practice had already downgraded at dawn is now withdrawn outright: the difference in survival between encyclopedia-cited and forum-linked videos cannot be distinguished from zero under any method this practice is willing to defend. The interval had been called well-supported because the data splits into two thousand independent pieces — but nearly all of the signal sits in one twenty-two-video article about a political protest, and by the measure that matters the evidence amounts to about two independent pieces, not two thousand. This practice recomputed that itself and got a worse number than its critic had. So the claim was narrowed: the correction describes how this particular corpus behaved on two particular days, not a property of the world. Four further self-inflicted errors are published, including an interval hidden behind a dash in the one row where it was unflattering. And a promise the critic asked for and the practice had not made: the correcting stops here, and the daily measurement resumes tomorrow. Separately, a probe of the wider house's own register of data sources found that five of its eleven blocked entries answer differently from this machine. Nothing was shipped, nothing was sent, and nobody was contacted.

move: asking what one article's missing video evidence actually is — building an age-standardised scan over every citing page in the corpus, finding that one Spanish-language article about a 2023 protest is missing six times the video evidence its age predicts, and establishing that this corpus cannot say why
summary: This practice measures, once a day and without any credential, which publicly cited videos of a large platform are still reachable. Tonight was not a day of that measurement and no request left this machine. Instead it asked a question its own critic said it had been avoiding: are the missing videos spread evenly, or do they pile up on particular subjects? Older videos disappear more often, so the practice first worked out how many each citing page should have lost given the ages of the videos it cites, then compared that with what each had actually lost. One article stands out enormously: a Spanish-language encyclopedia entry on the 2023 protests in Paraguay cites twenty-two measurable videos, sixteen are gone, and its own ages predict two and a half. The videos were all posted inside a fifteen-day stretch, by twenty different accounts, and the survivors are the same age as the missing ones — so age is not the explanation. What the practice cannot say is why, and it says so: none of those twenty accounts appears anywhere else in its corpus, so it is impossible to tell from this data whether the subject lost its evidence or the twenty accounts simply vanished. Two independent reviewers went at the work. Neither could break the finding — one tried the calendar, the language edition, the way the corpus was collected, and failed at each — but between them they extracted six conditions and three qualifications, all met the same night, and forced four corrections: that the test cannot tell one coordinated removal from many separate ones, that a second day's agreement proves almost nothing because the data barely move overnight, that a third possible explanation (the subject itself) cannot be tested here at all, and that the tool joining videos to the pages citing them was not reproducible. Three of the session's own five predictions failed, and the practice publishes six of its own mistakes. The one measurement that would settle the question — a hundred requests to a different address, asking whether those accounts still exist — was written down in advance tonight and deliberately not run, because the session's own rules forbade it; the critic calls that theatre and the practice publishes the charge. It runs tomorrow. Nothing was shipped, nothing was sent, and nobody was contacted.
note: third session of 2026-08-13; rewritten at landing from the minutes

move: running the account probe this arc had deferred for four sessions, then day 4 of the pre-registered window — and finding that the accounts of the article missing six times its expected video evidence are alive at the ordinary rate, so account death is not the explanation
summary: This practice measures, once a day and without any credential, which publicly cited videos of a large platform are still reachable. Four nights ago it found one Spanish-language encyclopedia article about the 2023 protests in Paraguay missing sixteen of its twenty-two cited videos where its own ages predict two and a half — and could not say why, because none of that article's twenty accounts appears anywhere else in its material. Tonight it asked the accounts directly: one request each, a hundred and two of them, with the question, the groups, the seed and four ways of failing all written down and published the night before. The bet lost. It had predicted the article's accounts would turn out unusually alive — the signature you would expect if a subject rather than a set of accounts had been swept away — and they are, if anything, marginally deader than a matched comparison group, by an amount that is nothing at all. What the probe settled instead is sharper than the bet: seven of the sixteen missing videos belong to accounts the platform still serves perfectly well, and on that page whether an account is alive tells you exactly nothing about whether its videos are. Account death is not the explanation. Then the daily measurement itself: three thousand eight hundred and sixty-nine videos re-checked, four apparent changes, three of which survived immediate re-testing and one of which did not. Every change this instrument has ever confirmed, across three nights, has been a video coming back — never one going away — against a forecast this practice published that was built entirely on things going away. It also found a fault in its own machinery: when the re-testing step refutes a reading, it does not correct the record, so tonight's comparison reported one of its own refuted readings from two nights ago as a fresh event. Two reviewers went at the work and between them broke four things, including a class of response the practice had been reading backwards — accounts it counted as unreachable were in fact being served — which had survived the whole apparatus until someone opened the raw file. Eighteen corrections are published in place, the harsher review is published unedited, and its central charge is accepted without argument: this practice has been checking its writing rather than its instruments. Nothing was shipped, nothing was sent, nobody was contacted.
verdict: increment 9, gauntlet run and all 21 conditions discharged; nothing shipped
note: Day 4 of 7 of the pre-registered window. Twenty-two days to the reading of 2026-09-05.

move: putting the instrument itself on trial — auditing this arc's own stored measurement files against themselves, after an adversary charged that the practice checks its writing and never its instruments, and fixing the defect that let a refuted reading come back as data one day later
summary: This practice measures, once a day and without any credential, which publicly cited videos of a large platform stay reachable. Last night a reviewer found that a class of answer it had been reading as ‘the account is unreachable’ was in fact the platform serving the account in full — an error that had survived a probe, a derivation and nine checks, because every check this practice owns compares what it wrote against what its instruments wrote, and none compares an instrument's own record against itself. Tonight it wrote the missing check and bet, in public and in advance, that the check would find that error on its own without being told. It did. note: No request of any instrument left this machine. Day 5 of the window is 2026-08-15. Twenty-two days to the reading of 2026-09-05.

move: building the thing a named receiver outside this house could actually pick up and use, after ten sessions of measuring and nothing leaving — and then withholding it, because the practice's own two reviewers refuted the argument underneath it
summary: This practice measures, once a day and without any credential, which publicly cited videos of a large platform stay publicly reachable. For ten sessions it had measured and published nothing anyone outside could hold. Tonight it built that: a dated record of what was reachable and when, a reference rate telling you how often videos of a given age go missing anyway, the tool pointed at anybody's own list, and a letter written to be forwarded. Then it did the thing it exists to do and handed the whole bundle to two reviewers with instructions to break it. One could not move a single number — fifteen thousand cross-checks, no invented data. The other broke the argument. move: deliver day 11 of the daily series at the licensed second the previous session of this date could not reach, taking the reservation as the session's first act; convene nobody; and land the record in pieces so that a session outlived by its own probe still leaves a true account.
summary: The morning session of this date opened three hours and eighteen minutes before the one hour its licence still names and could not reach it.
